finding: The header's exception list is a closed enumeration written against the pre-repair ruleset and carried forward unchanged over a repair that roughly tripled the document's mechanism. It reads: "Most rules below fired in a pilot run or were refuted by one; the exceptions are named where they sit — `UNVERIFIABLE` has zero pilot instances (§3), §7's storage decision rests on a probe rather than on a pilot run, and §9's advisory has no pilot instance at all." The repair added, with no pilot instance and no exception naming them: §4.1's reject-at-record tier floor, §7.1's exit codes, §7.2's ten-field row schema, §7.3's N-numbering and separate prefix list, §8's `text_sha` carry-forward, and §2.2's anchor-only emission. The sharpest case is §6, because there the repair narrowed an existing rule out of its own evidence: §6 now says the ranked-cause rule "is scoped to `QUESTION`", and `spec/working-map.md`'s Ground log records **zero** QUESTION rows in all four runs (1.52.0, 1.53.0, 0.37.1, 1.0.0 — 76 claims, QUESTION column 0/0/0/0). §6's one success story — "a field asserted to be driver-facing turned out to be written at two sites and read nowhere" — ended in a refutation, i.e. a FAIL, so under the new scope it is no longer an instance of the rule it is offered as evidence for. This is the shape the grounding pass already refuted once on this file (working-map: "a rule claimed to have 'fired or been refuted' in the pilot while the document's own §3 says that verdict has zero pilot instances"), reappearing after the repair.
suggestion: Either widen the header to "the rules in §2–§5 fired in a pilot run or were refuted by one; §4.1's tier floor, §6's ranked causes, §7 and §8 are designed and unexercised", or name §6 as a fourth exception beside §3, §7 and §9. If §6's rule is to keep its pilot evidence, do not scope it to `QUESTION` — scope it to "a claim the first attempt did not settle", which is what the three anchoring failures and the refutation actually were.

finding: §1.1 carries forward, verbatim in substance, a measured absence claim that this document's own review round falsified, and narrows it at the same time. New text: "Measured: `review_rounds` is empty for all three, and `spec/.tp-review/` holds no directory for any pending spec." Measured now: `ls spec/.tp-review/` returns 0.23.0 0.24.0 0.25.0 0.26.0 0.28.0 0.29.0 0.30.0 0.31.0 0.31.1 0.31.2 0.32.0 0.33.0 0.34.0 0.35.0 0.36.0 0.37.0 **1.0.0** — and 1.0.0 is a pending spec, whose directory holds `snapshot-round-1.md`, the very baseline this round diffs against. The document's own header now says it was "repaired by one review round", so the file asserts and denies the same fact three lines apart. The repair also DROPPED the baseline's second half — round 1 read "...for any pending spec or for the `0.38.0`–`0.54.0` files they were renamed from" — which was the half that made the absence claim complete, since a directory could survive under a pre-rename name. So the claim is now both narrower and false, and the surviving conclusion (the three pilot specs were never reviewed) is no longer supported by the sentence offered as its measurement.
suggestion: Restate the measurement over the set it is actually about: `review_rounds` is empty for 1.52.0, 1.53.0 and 0.37.1, and no `spec/.tp-review/` directory exists for any of the three or for the `0.38.0`–`0.54.0` names they were renamed from. Do not quantify over "any pending spec" — this file is one, and grounding it created the counterexample.

finding: Row 3's assertion is half a prohibition on the test suite itself — 'no test and no emitted string carries a count of this repository's own prose' — and its mutant is the ADDITION of such a test. Adding a test cannot make an existing test fail, so nothing in the suite goes red when the mutant lands. The only mechanism that would catch it is a guard scanning test sources for a count, i.e. a NotContains over unbounded text, which this repository has already measured as unable to pin what a document claims (two paragraphs re-adding a deleted promise passed green). So row 3 names a mutant that cannot fail it, for a different reason than rows 2 and 6 but with the same result.
suggestion: Delete row 3 and keep its rule where it already lives, as §2.1's decision — §11's header requires every row to name a code mutant and this rule admits none. If it must stay a test row, restate it as a code assertion with a code mutant: the derivation's parameter is prose text and never a path, so the mutant has to open a file inside the function, and assert that the ground package's non-test source contains no reference to the spec directory. Falsifier: name the guard that goes red when the mutant test is added; if it is a source scan, say so in the row and record the limit, which §11 does nowhere else.

finding: Row 4's mutant — inline the unit text — passes row 4's assertion. Clause one (the prompt carries (unit_id, line, first 60 chars) per unit and the spec path) is satisfied by an inlining implementation, which carries all of that plus the rest of the sentence; only a NotContains over unbounded prose would see the extra bytes. Clause two (byte size grows sub-linearly in the spec's prose bytes, asserted on two specs of different size) is satisfied by inlining too: anchors cost a constant ~75 bytes per unit and inlining costs ~1 byte per prose byte, but BOTH are affine in prose bytes (c·prose + header), so both have a ratio that falls as the fixed header amortises. Two data points cannot separate two affine functions by slope, and the sign of the comparison for the correct implementation depends on the two fixtures' average sentence length, so a correct implementation can fail the test while the mutant passes it.
suggestion: Replace the growth clause with a bounded read-back on a constructed fixture: a spec whose only prose is one 200-character sentence whose tail 140 characters are a unique nonce; assert the emitted prompt contains the first 60 characters and does not contain the nonce. The fixture is bounded and the nonce is unique, so this negation is not a blacklist inside an unbounded text. Falsifier: name two spec fixtures whose prompt/prose ratio comparison an inlining implementation reverses — if one exists, put it in the row.

finding: Row 6's mutant — compare tiers by equality rather than by order — passes every case row 6 asserts. Under equality: {kind: behaviour, tier: read} is rejected (the row expects rejected), {kind: behaviour, tier: run} is accepted (expects accepted), {kind: document, tier: read} is accepted (expects accepted). All three asserted rows carry a tier equal to or below their kind's minimum, so none of them can see the difference between == and >=. The single input that separates the two, {kind: document, tier: run, verdict: PASS}, appears only in the mutant column and is not asserted. §11's header says a mutant no input distinguishes from the shipped code is not a mutant, and §11's closing paragraph calls rows 6 and 7 the pair this release exists for.
suggestion: Add one accepted case whose tier is strictly ABOVE the kind's minimum — {kind: document, tier: run, verdict: PASS} — to row 6's assertion; that is the only shape that makes the ordering observable. Falsifier: exhibit an equality-comparison implementation that fails one of row 6's three currently asserted cases. None exists, which is the finding.

finding: 'units are split on `.`, `!` or `?` followed by whitespace and an opening character' leaves 'an opening character' undefined and never says whether lines are joined before splitting. This file is hard-wrapped near 100 columns, so most sentences cross a line break: under a per-line reading the split marker never appears mid-line and each prose LINE becomes a unit; under a join-then-split reading a sentence is a unit. Both are consistent with the paragraph and they produce different floors — which is §8's denominator, §7.1's --check, and every coverage figure the release reports. The same gap decides whether 'v0.36.0 §2.2 defines' or 'e.g.' or a trailing '`internal/cli/audit.go:355`.' splits.
suggestion: Give the rule to the precision of a regular expression, as this document does for the arms: join consecutive non-excluded lines into a paragraph, then split on [.!?] followed by whitespace and a character in a named class (for example [A-Z`*_"(§]). Add a §11 row over a fixture holding one hard-wrapped sentence, one abbreviation and one trailing code citation, with the mutant 'split per line'. Falsifier: apply both readings to §1.2's second paragraph and compare unit counts — they differ, so no test written from the current wording is reproducible by a second engineer.

finding: The floor rule is stated over LINES and the unit is a SENTENCE, and the spec never says the lines are joined first. "Prose is every line of the file except fenced blocks, headings, table rows and list markers; units are split on `.`, `!` or `?` followed by whitespace and an opening character." This corpus is hard-wrapped at ~100 columns, so nearly every sentence spans a line break, and the two readings are not close. I implemented the stated rule and swept the readings it admits: floor size on this file is 84 units when prose lines are joined into paragraphs before splitting and 130 when each line is split on its own (317 vs 138 total units) — the same rule, the same file, 1.5x on the denominator of §8's convergence gate. Two further undecided tokens move it again: "an opening character" is undefined (any non-whitespace gives 84, uppercase-only gives 73), and "list markers" does not say whether the marker alone is excluded or the whole line (84 vs 90 — the difference is §10's eight Non-Goals and §1.2's two bullets, i.e. whether the section where every decision in this spec is written owes eight `NOT-A-CLAIM` rows or is invisible to the floor). Full spread across six defensible readings: 73 to 130. §11 row 3 forbids the only test that would pin any of this — it requires the tests assert "the rule on constructed units" and names "assert the floor size of a `spec/*.md` file" as the mutant — and constructed single-line units exercise neither wrapping nor list markers, so every reading passes row 3 identically.
suggestion: Add three clauses to §2.1: (1) whether contiguous prose lines are joined into a paragraph before splitting (say "joined on a single space, paragraphs delimited by blank lines" or "each line is split independently"); (2) what "an opening character" is, as a character class; (3) whether a list-marker line contributes its remainder as prose or is excluded entirely. Then keep row 3's ban on a corpus FIGURE but allow a corpus INVARIANT test — e.g. a fixture with a known hard-wrapped sentence, a marker line and a nested fence, asserting the unit boundaries rather than the count.

finding: The repair deletes the path-citation arm — correctly — but replaces round 1's measured justification with a new one that is false, and pins a test to it. §2.1: "A citation in this repository's own registered form carries a line number — `internal/cli/audit.go:355` — so every unit the path arm would catch is already caught by the digit arm." The registered form is what `scripts/check-spec-code-citations.py` accepts, and its `PATH_CITE` (line 36) makes the line number OPTIONAL: `^([\w./\-]+\.(?:go|py|md|json|yml|yaml))(?::(\d+)(?:-(\d+))?)?$`. Measured over every backticked span in `spec/*.md`: **61** registered path citations carry `:N` and **645** do not (91%). The conclusion survives — a bare `internal/cli/audit.go` is still in the floor — but via the **identifier** (backtick) arm, not the digit arm, because the checker only ever looks inside backticks in the first place. Round 1's finding got this right by measuring units ("57 prose units hold a path citation and 0 of them lack a digit"); the repair replaced a measurement over units with an assertion about citation form, and the assertion is wrong for nine tenths of the corpus. Test 2 then inherits it: it asserts the unit "is in the floor via the **digit** arm", which is the wrong mechanism for the majority case.
suggestion: State the reason that holds: every citation the registered check sees is inside a backtick span, so the identifier arm subsumes the path arm regardless of whether a line number is present. Re-point test 2 at the identifier arm, or assert both arms independently with `internal/cli/audit.go:355` and a bare `internal/cli/audit.go`.

finding: §3 defines QUESTION's second shape as 'it succeeded below the claim's minimum tier', and §4.1 says QUESTION 'is precisely how a unit records that it could not reach the tier'. §7.2 admits tier only iff verdict is in {PASS, PARTIAL, FAIL} and evidence only iff tier is present. So a QUESTION row cannot record which tier it did reach, nor what it did — the thing §4.1 says it exists to record. The two QUESTION shapes are indistinguishable in the record, no test can tell an ambiguous failure from a read that was not enough, and the release's headline case (a behavioural claim confirmed by reading) leaves no evidence of the reading behind. This is the same shape as round 1's partial_kind gap: that half was closed by adding a field, this half was not.
suggestion: Admit tier and evidence on a QUESTION row as optional and unconstrained by the minimum, or add question_kind with values {ambiguous-failure, below-minimum-tier} and one §11 row asserting a below-minimum QUESTION records the tier it reached and is not rejected. Falsifier: name the field a unit writes to say 'I read it, and reading is not evidence here' — §7.2 has none.

finding: The repair moved a verdict assignment and left the sentence written against the old assignment standing one subsection above it. Baseline §4.1: "a probe whose subject is a package-internal symbol cannot be run in a copy; that claim is `QUESTION` and its row says which tier it failed on." New §4.2: "That claim is `UNVERIFIABLE` — no evidence at the required tier is obtainable — not `QUESTION`." That change is declared. But new §4.1 still reads: "`QUESTION`, `UNVERIFIABLE` and `NOT-A-CLAIM` carry no such constraint — **`QUESTION` is precisely how a unit records that it could not reach the tier.**" The package-internal case IS a unit that could not reach the tier, so §4.1 says QUESTION and §4.2 says not-QUESTION about the same input. §3 draws the real line (QUESTION = succeeded BELOW the minimum tier; UNVERIFIABLE = no evidence at the required tier obtainable AT ALL), and §4.1's sentence collapses it. Second, the old decision's other half was dropped without notice: "its row says which tier it failed on" is now unrecordable, because §7.2 requires `tier` and `evidence` only when the verdict is PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL. An UNVERIFIABLE row therefore cannot say which tier it could not reach — exactly the diagnostic §4.2's limit paragraph exists to preserve.
suggestion: Scope §4.1's sentence to the case §3 gives it: "`QUESTION` is how a unit records that it settled the claim only below the minimum tier; `UNVERIFIABLE` is how it records that the tier is unreachable." Then either make `tier` required (or add a `tier_unreached` field) for UNVERIFIABLE in §7.2, or state in §4.2 that the tier is deliberately not recorded for it.

finding: Two sinks state the tier-minimum rule with different scopes, and `PARTIAL` falls in the gap. §4.1: "A `PASS` or `FAIL` recorded below its kind's minimum is rejected at record (exit 1)" — PARTIAL is not named. §7.1's exit-1 text drops the scope: "a row fails validation — ... or a tier below its kind's minimum (§4.1)", which reads as every row carrying a tier. §7.2 requires `tier` on PARTIAL. §11 row 6 tests only PASS, so no test distinguishes them. The implementer must decide whether `{kind: behaviour, tier: read, verdict: PARTIAL}` records, and the two answers differ in what the release is worth: if it records, every claim a unit cannot reach by running is downgraded from FAIL to PARTIAL and the read stands in for the run anyway — the precise evasion §4.1's last paragraph says the mechanism exists to close. PARTIAL is not a marginal verdict here: §3 gives it three sub-kinds and the pilot produced two of them in one run.
suggestion: Scope the rule once, in §4.1, over the set §7.2 requires a tier for: "A PASS, PARTIAL or FAIL recorded below its kind's minimum is rejected at record." Then make §7.1's exit-1 line quote that set rather than restating it. Add the boundary row to §11 row 6: `{kind: behaviour, tier: read, verdict: PARTIAL}` rejected, with the mutant "scope the check to PASS and FAIL, which leaves PARTIAL as an unguarded downgrade path".

finding: §4.1 declares the six tiers "totally ordered as listed" and each kind a MINIMUM, so any tier at or above it is accepted. That admits `{kind: behaviour, tier: probe, verdict: PASS}` — probe outranks run — and §4.2 defines a probe as something built and run "in a copy the unit makes for itself, OUTSIDE the repository". The artifact producing the evidence is then, by construction, not the artifact the claim is about. The order conflates two dimensions: `read`/`query`/`run` rank depth ON THE REAL SUBJECT, while `probe`/`red-green`/`break-and-control` rank rigour on a CONSTRUCTED subject, and past `run` "higher" means "different subject". §4's own opening paragraph is the falsifying instance already in the document: the `-type d` digest pipeline "read perfectly and changed nothing whatsoever when executed" — proxy reasoning about a mechanism, which is exactly what a probe substitutes for a run. Row 6's mutant considers and rejects equality-comparison as "over-strict where the defect is under-strict"; nobody constructed the under-strict input the ORDER itself admits, and it defeats the pair §11 says the release exists for.
suggestion: Falsifier: an argument that a purpose-built probe is evidence about existing shipped behaviour — §4's first sentence ("only running is evidence about behaviour", where running means the shipped command per the `run` tier's own definition) denies it. Replace the per-kind MINIMUM with a per-kind ACCEPTABLE-TIER SET: `behaviour` accepts {run, red-green, break-and-control} but not `probe`; `mechanism` accepts {probe, red-green, break-and-control} but not `run`. A set is still a closed enum a test can read back, and it costs one table column. Then add a row asserting `{behaviour, probe}` is rejected — an input no current row reaches.

finding: §4.2 is the only normative subsection §11 does not reach, and it is the one making half the tier table achievable. Its decision is that `tp ground` emits its OWN isolation clause, because the shipped one (`internal/cli/clauses.go:19`, quoted correctly in §4.2) "forbids the probe the tier table requires". §4.2 then promises an assertion — "the ground suffix gets its own" — that §11 does not contain: the seventeen rows derive from §2.1 (1,2,3), §2.2 (4), §3 (5), §4.1 (6,7), §6 (8,9), §7.2 (10), §7.3 (11,12,13), §7.1 (14), §8 (15,16) and §9 (17). Nothing from §4.2. The consequence is concrete: an implementation that appends the EXISTING `isolationClause` passes all seventeen rows, including 6 and 7, because those validate a recorded `tier` VALUE and never check that the emitted prompt permits reaching it. The tiers `probe`, `red-green` and `break-and-control` — the minimums for `mechanism`, `defect` and `guard` — then become unreachable in practice while the record still accepts them, which is the reverse of the failure §4.1 is built to prevent. §11's preamble is "every row derives from a numbered decision", not the converse, so this gap is invisible from inside §11.
suggestion: Falsifier: any of rows 1-17 that a wrong clause fails — I traced all seventeen against "append `clauseSuffix()` unchanged" and none does. Add two rows: (a) the ground suffix asserted byte for byte, and asserted NOT equal to `clauseSuffix()`; (b) `clauseSuffix()` itself unchanged, so v0.36.0 §6.2's assertion still holds. Both are bounded-artifact assertions (a constant compared whole), the shape this project has recorded as the only one a rewording cannot slip past. Also correct §4.2's count while there: `clauses.go:5,17,21` records isolationClause as v0.36.0 §2.2 and incrementalClause as §3.2, so §2.2 defines ONE constant, not "the two v0.36.0 §2.2 defines".

finding: §4.2 requires a third clause constant beside the two v0.36.0 defines, and gives its text only as a paraphrase: it "permits writing inside a copy the unit creates outside the repository and forbids every write inside it except the round's own output file". It then requires a byte-level assertion over it — "the ground suffix gets its own" — so a test must pin bytes the spec never states. This repository has already recorded why that fails: `internal/cli/clauses.go:11-15` says the two shipped clauses are given as fenced blocks because "a hard-wrapped blockquote left an implementer three transcription choices (join with a space, join with \n, keep or strip the \"> \" prefixes), each producing a different artefact and each passing a loose reading of 'verbatim'". A prose paraphrase is strictly weaker than the hard-wrapped blockquote that produced that lesson, and the clause is not decorative: it is the only thing overriding the shipped `isolationClause` (`clauses.go:19`), whose text §4.2 itself quotes verbatim because it had to.
suggestion: Give the ground clause as a fenced block containing the exact single line, as v0.36.0 §2.2 does for the other two. Also state the suffix's assembly order explicitly (ground clause then `incrementalClause`, or the reverse) — §4.2 says "appended together with `incrementalClause` unchanged" without fixing the order, and the byte-for-byte test cannot be written without it.

finding: §6 scopes the three-to-five ranked causes to QUESTION and justifies it as "what a unit does INSTEAD of guessing" — the pilot's three anchoring instances are all diagnoses of a FAILURE whose reason was unknown. §3's repair then gave QUESTION a second shape with no unknown in it: "it succeeded below the claim's minimum tier". There the unit knows the single cause exactly — it read where a run was required — and §7.2 makes `causes` required "iff verdict is QUESTION", with row 8 pinning length 2 as rejected and 3 as accepted. So a hard lower bound of three falsifiable `{cause, prediction}` pairs is imposed on a shape with one known cause, which forces the unit to manufacture two more. §6's own sentence names the result: "A cause with no prediction is a vibe." The rule designed to stop guessing now requires it, and the mechanism has no way to tell a genuine ranked diagnosis from three filler rows, so row 8's count check certifies the fabrication rather than catching it. §3 explicitly reasoned about this trade for PARTIAL — three shapes, one verdict, a `partial_kind` subfield — and the same reasoning was not re-run for QUESTION after the repair widened it.
suggestion: Falsifier: a worked example of three ranked, falsifiable causes for the case "behavioural claim confirmed by reading, run not attempted" — if one exists this finding is wrong, and putting it in §6 settles it either way. Otherwise scope `causes` to the ambiguous-failure shape only (paired with the `question_kind` discriminator §7.2 needs anyway), and require the reached `tier` + `evidence` instead on the tier-shortfall shape, where they are the informative content. Row 8's bound then applies to the shape it was designed for, and a second row should assert that a tier-shortfall QUESTION with zero causes is ACCEPTED — an input no current row reaches.

finding: Exit 2 is defined as 'usage, including --record without --status's companion flags'. §7.1's own table lists 'tp ground <spec> --record <file>' as a valid invocation carrying no --status, so the sentence declares a usage error out of an invocation the table two lines above declares valid; and '--status's companion flags' names no flag — the only companion of --status in the table is --check, which --record does not take. Row 14 requires each of 0/1/2/3/4 to be 'produced by a named input, one test per code', and for code 2 no input is derivable: one engineer writes 'tp ground s.md --record r.ndjson' expecting 2 and another writes the same command expecting 0.
suggestion: Replace the clause with the usage errors the table actually implies — --check without --status, --record together with --status, --record with no file argument — and let row 14 cite one by name. Falsifier: a reading under which 'tp ground <spec> --record <file>' is simultaneously the table's second row and a usage error.

finding: §7.1 breaks the exit-code promise this same repair wrote into §1.2, in the same document. §7.1: "Exit codes follow tp's existing table with no additions: ... **4** the state directory is unreadable or holds a malformed ground round." tp's existing table is `internal/cli/exitcodes.go:5-9`: 0 success, 1 ExitValidation, 2 ExitUsage, 3 ExitFile, **4 ExitState — "wrong status transition, blocked task, no ready tasks for --first"**. The corrupt-state-directory outcome is already assigned, and it is assigned to 3, not 4: `exitStateError` in `internal/cli/review_record.go` does `output.Error(ExitFile, ce.Error(), ce.Hint())` / `os.Exit(ExitFile)` for an `engine.StateCorruptError`, which is the path both `tp review --record` and `tp audit --record` take. §1.2's own bullet — new in this repair — reads "an exit code already assigned to an outcome keeps that outcome". §7.1 moves the corrupt-state outcome from 3 to 4 and calls that "no additions", so the release that introduces the 1.x exit-code promise violates it in the section that states its own codes. Separately, the exit-2 gloss is not parseable: "usage, including `--record` without `--status`'s companion flags" — `--record` and `--status` are alternative invocations in the table above it, so no such combination exists.
suggestion: Map a corrupt or unreadable ground-round directory to **3**, matching `exitStateError`, and drop the 4 row (or state explicitly that 4 is being newly assigned to an outcome that had none, which §1.2's second sentence permits and the "no additions" claim contradicts). Replace the exit-2 gloss with a real usage case, e.g. `--check` without `--status`.

finding: The required-field column is written as a biconditional — "`tier` | iff verdict ∈ {PASS, PARTIAL, FAIL}" — which forbids `tier` on a `QUESTION` row. §3 defines QUESTION's second shape as "it succeeded below the claim's minimum tier", and §3 calls that shape "the one this release exists for". So the row that carries the release's headline signal cannot record the tier that made it a QUESTION: the fact is known, is the whole content of the verdict, and has no cell. §4.1 says the opposite in different words — "`QUESTION`, `UNVERIFIABLE` and `NOT-A-CLAIM` carry no such constraint" waives the MINIMUM, which presupposes a tier may be present. A validator cannot be written: `{verdict: QUESTION, kind: behaviour, tier: read}` is rejected under §7.2 and legal under §4.1, and §11 has no row for it.
suggestion: Make the tier row read "required iff verdict ∈ {PASS, PARTIAL, FAIL}; optional for QUESTION, where it records the tier actually reached and no minimum applies; forbidden otherwise" — and add a test row asserting `{verdict: QUESTION, kind: behaviour, tier: read}` records, with the mutant "reject it, which loses the only record of how far the attempt got".

finding: `anchor` is required on every row, typed `string` with no null, and defined as "the `§n(.n)*` section the unit sits in" — but §2.2 settles that a unit travels as `(unit_id, line, first 60 characters)`, which carries no section, so nothing says who derives the anchor or from what. Worse, the value does not exist for every floor unit. Measured on this spec: two floor units sit in the blockquote at lines 3-7, before `## 1. Overview`. Blockquotes are not in §2.1's exclusion list (fenced blocks, headings, table rows, list markers), so those lines are prose; both units carry digits and backticks, so both are in the floor; and neither sits in any `§n` section. A conforming unit therefore cannot write a valid row for them, `--record` rejects whatever it writes (exit 1, "a missing required field"), and `tp ground spec/1.0.0.md --status --check` can never exit 0 on this spec — the release's own document is permanently uncoverable by its own gate.
suggestion: Either make `anchor` `string | null` with "null for a unit preceding the first section heading", or have tp compute and emit the anchor as a fourth element of the tuple (`(unit_id, anchor, line, first 60 chars)`) with a defined value for pre-heading prose, e.g. `§0`. Say which side computes it. A test row belongs with it: a floor unit above the first heading records.

finding: `text_sha` is a required field on every row — 'first 12 hex of the sha256 of the unit's text as emitted' — but §2.2 emits only `(unit_id, line, first 60 characters)`, so the unit is never given the text it must hash. To produce a matching value it has to re-implement §2.1's tokenizer byte-for-byte: the fence/heading/table/list exclusion, the joining of wrapped prose lines (§2.1 never says whether they are joined, or with what), the `.`/`!`/`?` + whitespace + 'an opening character' split (undefined), and whether terminal punctuation stays on the unit. Every disagreement produces a non-matching sha, and under §8 a non-matching sha means the unit is uncovered — so the failure is silent and its price is exactly the cost §8 exists to avoid: a full re-decide of the floor. Measured on this file at 446 lines: 84 floor units; the 3-tuple anchor payload is 5,669 B and adding a 12-hex sha per unit costs 1,092 B (+19%), against a re-decide worth 84 dispositions. tp already holds every one of those hashes, because it emitted the text they are over. Falsifier: a sentence pinning §2.1's line-joining and split precisely enough that two independent implementations agree byte-for-byte, or a sentence saying tp emits the sha — neither is present, and the second is the cheap one.
suggestion: Make the anchor a 4-tuple: `(unit_id, line, text_sha, first 60 characters)`, and say in §7.2 that the unit copies `text_sha` back for a floor unit and computes it only for a reader-added claim (`unit_id: null`), which is the one case tp genuinely cannot know. §2.2's 'Each unit travels as (unit_id, line, first 60 characters)' and §11 row 4's three-field assertion both need the fourth field named. What the row cannot carry: this is not a byte-shaving preference — it is the difference between §8's carry-forward being computable and being a hash the two sides derive independently and are never told to compare, which is the failure mode that reports 100% uncovered while looking correct.

finding: `text_sha` is defined as "the sha256 of the unit's text as emitted", and §2.2 settles that the emitted text is NOT the unit — each unit travels as `(unit_id, line, first 60 characters)`. So "as emitted" resolves to the 60-character prefix, and an implementer who reads it that way ships a hash blind to everything past character 60. Measured on this spec under the §2.1 rule: 84 floor units, of which 90% exceed 60 characters and the longest is 506. Under that reading §8's carry-forward silently reuses a disposition across a sentence that was rewritten from character 61 onward — which is the exact defect §8 says `text_sha` exists to prevent. §11 row 16 does not discriminate: it asserts "a unit whose text changed by one character does not carry forward", and that passes under BOTH readings whenever the changed character happens to sit inside the first 60. The other reading (hash the full sentence) is also buildable and gives a different on-disk value, so two conforming implementations produce incompatible rounds.
suggestion: State which string is hashed, in one clause: "the sha256 of the unit's full sentence text, not of the 60-character anchor". Then fix row 16's mutant so it can fail — require the changed character to be at an offset beyond the emitted prefix (e.g. a unit longer than 60 chars whose only edit is at character 120), which is the input that separates the two readings.

finding: `text_sha` is required on EVERY row ("first 12 hex of the sha256 of the unit's text as emitted"), and the unit that writes the row never receives that text. §2.2 fixes the emission exactly: "tp emits the floor as anchors, never as text. Each unit travels as `(unit_id, line, first 60 characters)`" — three elements, no hash, and 60 characters of a sentence this repository hard-wraps across two to four physical lines. To produce the hash the unit must re-implement §2.1's split (`.`/`!`/`?` + whitespace + opening char) AND a canonical form the spec never states: whether the wrap newline becomes a space, whether leading indentation is stripped, whether a blockquote's `> ` prefix is stripped, whether the trailing terminator is included. Two conforming implementations disagree. Worse, the failure is SILENT: §7.2 constrains `text_sha`'s type, not its value, so a wrong-but-well-formed hash is accepted, §8's carry-forward simply never fires, and pass N+1 re-decides the whole floor — precisely the cost §8 says the field exists to avoid ("twelve full passes where the design intends one and eleven scoped ones"). Row 16 asserts carry-forward on unchanged text but never asserts that a UNIT-supplied hash equals tp's, so it passes with tp's own hash on both sides of the join and never exercises the derivation the unit is actually required to perform.
suggestion: Falsifier: a place in §2.2 or §7 where tp hands the unit the canonical text or its hash — there is none. Cheapest fix: extend §2.2's anchor tuple to `(unit_id, line, text_sha, first 60 characters)`. tp already computed the hash to emit the floor, the cost is 12 hex per unit against the 60 characters already sent, and the unit echoes rather than derives. Keep "the unit supplies it for a reader-added claim", and add to §7.2 that a row whose `unit_id` is non-null and whose `text_sha` does not match the emitted floor is rejected — which turns the field from unverifiable to a bounded read-back. Add a row: a unit echoing a wrong hash for a known `unit_id` is rejected at record.

finding: anchor is required and typed as 'the §n(.n)* section the unit sits in', but this file's opening blockquote (lines 3-7) is prose under §2.1's rule — it is not a fenced block, a heading, a table row or a list marker — and its sentences carry digits and backticks, so they are floor units sitting ABOVE '## 1. Overview'. No §n(.n)* value exists for them. Their rows are therefore rejected at record (§7.2's 'a row failing any cell of this table is rejected'), the round is not written at all (§7.2's atomicity clause), and coverage on this very spec can never reach 100% — an outcome no §11 row would catch, because none tests the anchor field.
suggestion: Either exclude everything above the first heading from prose in §2.1, or define an anchor value for the preamble (§0) in §7.2 and say tp emits it. Add a §11 row asserting a preamble unit records and coverage reaches 100% on a fixture that has one. Falsifier: show the preamble lines are excluded by §2.1's list as written — they are not, blockquote lines appear in neither the inclusion nor the four exclusions.

finding: text_sha is required on every row and defined as 'the sha256 of the unit's text as emitted', but §2.2 emits '(unit_id, line, first 60 characters)' — the unit's text is never emitted. Both readings break a §11 row. If 'as emitted' means the 60-character prefix, row 16's 'a unit whose text changed by one character does not [carry forward]' is FALSE for any edit after character 60, and a test built on a late-sentence edit fails a correct implementation. If it means the full sentence, the unit must re-run §2.1's split rule by hand to recover text tp did not give it, and any disagreement in the split silently yields a non-matching hash and a unit that is uncovered forever with no error. The parenthetical 'the unit supplies it for a reader-added claim' also implies tp supplies it otherwise, which contradicts 'required: yes' on a row the unit writes.
suggestion: Emit the hash in the anchor tuple — (unit_id, line, text_sha, first 60 characters) — and say the unit copies it back verbatim for a floor unit and computes it only for a reader-added claim; then row 16's one-character mutation is over text tp itself hashed. Falsifier: state that tp fills text_sha at record from unit_id, which closes it the other way and makes the field not one the unit supplies at all.

finding: §7.2 makes `tier` required "iff verdict ∈ {PASS, PARTIAL, FAIL}" and `evidence` required "iff `tier` is present". Both are therefore FORBIDDEN on a QUESTION row. But §3's second QUESTION shape is defined BY the tier that was reached — "it succeeded below the claim's minimum tier" — and §11's closing paragraph calls rows 6/7 "the pair this release exists for", whose whole subject is that a read stood in for a run. So the row produced by the release's central case records `{kind: behaviour, verdict: QUESTION, causes: [...]}` and CANNOT record that a read was performed, what was read, or which tier was reached. §4.1's sentence "`QUESTION` is precisely how a unit records that it could not reach the tier" is false of the schema §7.2 defines: the row records that a tier was not reached and nothing about the one that was. The two QUESTION shapes are also indistinguishable on the record, while PARTIAL's three shapes got `partial_kind` — §3 reasoned explicitly about that asymmetry for PARTIAL and never for QUESTION, which acquired its second shape in this repair.
suggestion: Falsifier: any §7 field carrying the reached tier on a QUESTION row — there is none; §7.2 is the complete row schema and `note` is free text a test cannot read back. Make `tier` and `evidence` OPTIONAL on QUESTION (present for the tier-shortfall shape, absent for the ambiguous-failure shape), or add a `question_kind` enum mirroring `partial_kind` with the tier required on the `below-minimum-tier` member. If the tier-shortfall shape is deliberately unrecordable, say so and delete §4.1's sentence, because as written §4.1 and §7.2 describe different records.

finding: The carry-forward reads 'a unit whose text_sha matches a disposition in the previous round carries it forward'. Nothing says whether a carried disposition is re-written into round N's own file or only computed at --status, and nothing says whether the lookup is round N-1 alone or every earlier round. The readings diverge at round 3: a unit dispositioned in round 1 and unchanged since has no row in round 2 under the compute-at-status reading, so under 'the previous round' it becomes uncovered at round 3 and coverage falls with no edit to the spec. Row 16 asserts carry-forward over two rounds, which is exactly the fixture on which every reading agrees, and §7.1's --check ('every emitted floor unit carries a disposition') inherits the same undecidability.
suggestion: State one rule: the lookup walks every earlier ground round and takes the highest-numbered round carrying a matching text_sha, and coverage is computed over that union rather than over round N's file. Then row 16's fixture must be three rounds, not two. Falsifier: a three-round fixture on which both readings give the same coverage — none exists once any unit survives two rounds unchanged.

finding: §8 justifies `text_sha` on a saving it never measures — 'pass N re-decides the whole floor, which on a twelve-round cycle is twelve full passes where the design intends one and eleven scoped ones' — and §10 Non-Goal 8 then declines a round budget entirely because '§8's second pass shrinks by construction'. Measured on the only instance that exists, this spec's own round-1→round-2 repair (`git show 1344652b:spec/1.0.0.md`, 13 commits, 333→445 lines): applying §2.1's arms to both texts gives a round-1 floor of 63 units and a round-2 floor of 84, of which **13 carry forward by identical text and 71 (84.5%) are new or changed**. The scoped pass therefore saves 14% of the emit bytes (5,526 → 4,730) and 15% of the rows (84 → 71). §8's own cited figure predicts this rather than contradicting it: at a median repair locality of 70.2%, a repair round rewrites the text the next round reads. So 'shrinks by construction' is false as an economy — it shrinks by construction only in the sense that it is non-increasing — and Non-Goal 8 declines a bound on a loop with no demonstrated narrowing, on a per-round cost of ~5.7 KB emitted plus 84 dispositions. Falsifier: a later repair round on this or any spec whose carry-forward is high — one measurement settles it, and the derivation above is one command.
suggestion: Two separable fixes, and the first is free. (1) Delete the 'one full pass and eleven scoped ones' framing from §8 and keep `text_sha` on the correctness argument it actually earns — that nothing else joins a recorded disposition to a sentence — per §2.1's own precedent of stating the rule and refusing the figure. (2) Either restore a bound (a `ground_max_rounds`, or simply 'grounding runs once per review round and its cost is the changed units') or state in Non-Goal 8 that the loop is unbounded and why that is acceptable. What the row cannot carry: the sharper point is that the scoping saves tp's bookkeeping, not the unit's work — §7.1 says `tp ground <spec>` 'emits one prompt carrying the floor's anchors' with no marking of which units already carry a disposition, so the unit re-reads and re-decides all 84 every round and tp discards the matches at coverage time. Marking the already-dispositioned units in the emitted prompt is one bit per unit tp already holds, and it is what turns §8's claimed saving into a real one.

finding: §8's denominator is "what tp emitted" and asserts "tp knows that set exactly, because it produced it" — but nothing in the spec persists the emitted set, and §7.3 puts the snapshot at record rather than at emit. §7.3 says the first `--record` "must create `spec/.tp-review/<base>/` holding only the ground round and its snapshot", and §11 row 12 repeats it: "`--record` ... writes the round and its snapshot". This inverts the shipped convention without saying so — `snapshotPrefixes` in `internal/engine/reviewstate.go:316` is documented as "the artifacts an emission writes before any round is recorded". The consequence is concrete: at `--record` time tp has no record of what it emitted, so it must re-derive the floor from the spec file as it stands then, and `unit_id` — "the id tp assigned at emit" (§7.2) — cannot be validated against anything. If the spec was edited between emit and record (which §8 says is the normal case: "a review repair rewrites part of the spec"), the denominator is a set the unit never saw, and coverage is computed over a different floor than the one dispositioned. That is the defect the emit-time-hash release exists to close, being introduced fresh here.
suggestion: Decide and state where the emitted floor is persisted. The cheapest option consistent with §7.3's Non-Goals is: emit writes `snapshot-ground-round-N.md` (matching review/audit, and matching the prefix list §7.3 already reserves for it), and `--record` derives both the denominator and the legal `unit_id` set from that snapshot rather than from the live spec. Then say so in §8's denominator sentence, and add a test row: a spec edited between emit and record still records against the emitted floor.

finding: Non-Goal 3's justification survived a §3 repair that destroys it. §9: "The false-positive rate of 'ungrounded' is unknown, because §2.2 makes the floor deliberately imprecise, so a coverage gate would fail on units the reader correctly dispositioned `NOT-A-CLAIM`." That argument was sound in the baseline, where the vocabulary was five verdicts and a not-a-claim unit had no recordable value, so an over-wide floor really did strand units outside coverage. The repair added `NOT-A-CLAIM` as a sixth verdict precisely so that it does not — §2.2: "returns a disposition for every unit in it — one of §3's six values, `NOT-A-CLAIM` included"; §8: "Coverage is dispositions over the emitted floor." A unit correctly dispositioned `NOT-A-CLAIM` is therefore COVERED, and a coverage gate would not fail on it. The same repair also removes the premise of the first clause: once the denominator is "what tp emitted", "ungrounded" means "a unit tp emitted that carries no disposition", a set tp computes exactly, so it has no false-positive rate at all. The release's reason for not gating is now a sentence about a design it no longer has.
suggestion: Give Non-Goal 3 a reason that survives the six-verdict vocabulary — e.g. the floor's recall is untested, so a gate would refuse on a spec whose real claims the arms missed (§2.2 says these are invisible by construction), and no pilot run has measured that rate. Delete the false-positive-rate clause, which the emitted-floor denominator makes vacuous.

finding: Row 11 asserts that hasRecordedRoundFiles and hasStateArtifacts 'return what they returned before' a ground round. On a fixture that already holds a review round both return true before and after, so the named mutant — adding ground-round- to roundFilePrefixes — passes the row unchanged. The discriminating fixture is named only in the mutant column ('makes a ground-only spec read as having review state'), not in the assertion, so the row as written admits a test that cannot fail. This is the same defect as row 6's, in a row nobody would look at twice.
suggestion: Put the fixture in the assertion: on a spec with no prior review or audit round, both predicates return false before the ground round AND false after it, and tp resume reports the same phase either side. Falsifier: run the mutant against a fixture carrying a review round — both predicates return true with and without it, which is the input this row currently permits.

finding: Row 2 declares its own mutant behaviourally null — 're-add a path arm, which changes no unit's membership' — so the row's whole discriminating power sits in two structural claims about the implementation: 'the floor function exposes exactly three arms' and a unit is in the floor 'via the digit arm'. §2.1 requires neither. It defines membership only ('a unit is in the floor when it holds any of three arms'), which an implementation satisfies as a single boolean expression; against that implementation neither clause is assertable and the mutant is undetectable. §11's header says every row derives from a numbered decision, and this row's assertable half derives from none.
suggestion: Either add the requirement to §2.1 — the derivation exposes its arms as an enumerable set and reports which arm(s) matched a unit, so a length check kills the mutant — or delete row 2, since §2.1's paragraph already argues that no fourth arm can change membership and a row whose mutant is declared to change nothing is the class the header says it purged. Falsifier: an implementation of §2.1 exactly as worded that makes 'exposes exactly three arms' a readable value with no further requirement.

finding: Row 4 pins the anchors decision on an assertion that cannot decide it: 'its byte size grows sub-linearly in the spec's prose bytes — asserted on two specs of different size'. Measured over all 53 files in `spec/*.md` by applying §2.1's arms and pricing `(unit_id, line, first 60 chars)` per floor unit: the log-log fit of anchor bytes against prose bytes has slope **0.930**, and the anchors/prose ratio is a flat band — min 0.090, median 0.309, max 0.671. The payload is a roughly constant fraction of prose, not sub-linear, because the 60-character cap bounds the per-unit cost while the unit count still grows linearly with the document. Worse, the assertion is decided by fixture choice: of the 1,378 spec pairs, **622 (45.1%) yield a two-point exponent greater than 1**, so a conforming implementation passes or fails row 4 on which two specs the test picks, and either verdict is reproducible. This is the fixture-property trap this repository has already paid for. Falsifier: a stated pair of specs plus the exponent they yield — with the pair named, the row becomes checkable and, on this corpus, most named pairs would refute it.
suggestion: Assert the property the design delivers rather than one it does not. Two are directly checkable and neither depends on fixture choice: no emitted unit's text field exceeds 60 characters, and the emitted payload's size is bounded by k × (floor unit count) with k a stated constant — both hold by construction of §2.2 and both fail under the mutant row 4 already names (inlining the unit text). If a size comparison is wanted, state it as the ratio the decision actually buys: measured 2.89× on this file (16,358 B inlined against 5,669 B as anchors) and 1.24×–3.51× across the corpus. What the row cannot carry: the anchors decision is right and the saving is real — what is wrong is only the property the test names, and a green test naming the wrong property is how the next release justifies undoing it.

finding: Rows 10 and 12 give contradictory answers for the first --record on a fresh spec when that round holds one invalid row. Row 10 requires no file to be written and 'the directory' to be byte-identical to before the attempt; row 12 requires --record on a spec with no spec/.tp-review/<base>/ to create it. Under row 12 the directory exists afterwards, which is not byte-identical to its prior non-existence; under row 10 it does not, which §7.3's unconditional 'the first --record on a fresh spec must create' does not permit. Row 10 also never names which directory it means — the round directory or the working tree.
suggestion: Name the directory in row 10 (spec/.tp-review/<base>/) and add the missing clause to §7.3: a --record whose validation fails creates nothing, so on a fresh spec the directory is still absent afterwards. Then row 10's fixture can be the fresh-spec case and it strengthens rather than contradicts row 12. Falsifier: state instead that the directory is created before validation runs — that also resolves it, and makes row 10's byte-identity false as written.

finding: Two assertions the baseline's test table carried are gone and nothing replaces them; the §11 preamble accounts for only one of the removals. Baseline row 7: "recording a round writes `ground-round-N.ndjson` and leaves `state.json` **byte-identical**". The new table splits row 7 into rows 11, 12 and 13, and none of them asserts byte-identity of an EXISTING `state.json`: row 11 asserts `hasRecordedRoundFiles`/`hasStateArtifacts`/`tp resume` are unchanged (a prefix-list property, satisfiable while the file's bytes change), row 12 asserts only that no `state.json` is CREATED on a fresh spec, row 13 is numbering. So Non-Goal 2 ("No `state.json` key") — the decision §7.3 spends a paragraph justifying with the `SaveReviewState` typed-struct measurement — is untested for every spec that already has a `state.json`, which is every spec this release's ordering does not reach first. The preamble justifies replacing rows 1 and 10 of the earlier draft; it says nothing about row 7's byte-identity clause, which was not one of the two unfailable mutants.
suggestion: Add a row: recording a ground round on a spec whose `spec/.tp-review/<base>/state.json` already exists leaves that file byte-identical; mutant — index the ground round in `state.json`, which an older binary then drops on its next write (the baseline's own row-7 mutant, still valid).

finding: §11's header defines the fourth column as a mutant, and defines a mutant against 'the shipped code'. Three rows put a weaker TEST there instead of a code change: row 3 ('assert the floor size of a spec/*.md file'), row 8 ('assert only that a bare QUESTION with zero causes is rejected') and row 14 ('assert only success'). A weaker test does not fail the row's assertion, it replaces it, so those three rows carry no check on the code in the column that exists for exactly that. Rows 8 and 14 have sound assertions; only their mutant column is empty of content, which matters because the mutant column is what a reader uses to judge whether the assertion is at the right place.
suggestion: Name the code mutant each boundary pair actually catches. Row 8: 'accept 2 through 6' (dies on the length-2 case) and 'bound below only' (dies on the length-6 case). Row 14: 'collapse 3 and 4 onto 1', which every code but 0 reaches today. Row 3: see the separate finding. Falsifier: a reading of 'mutant' under which a weaker test is one — §11's own second sentence ('no input distinguishes from the shipped code') forecloses it.

finding: 'Prose is every line of the file except fenced blocks, headings, table rows and list markers' is ambiguous in two ways that move the floor. 'list markers' reads either as the marker token (so §10's eight Non-Goals are prose once the '1. ' is stripped) or as the whole list item (so all of §10 is outside the floor) — and §10's items do carry assertions, e.g. '§7.3's separate prefix list is what keeps that true'. Blockquotes appear in neither the inclusion nor the exclusions, and this file opens with one. §11 has no row over the exclusion set at all, so the one rule that fixes the denominator is the one rule with no test.
suggestion: Enumerate the exclusions as line predicates — fenced block, ATX heading, a line whose first non-space character is '|', a line whose first non-space token matches the list-marker pattern, a line whose first non-space character is '>' — and say whether an excluded line is dropped whole or stripped of its marker. Add a §11 row asserting one unit of each excluded kind is absent from the floor, with the mutant 'drop one predicate'. Falsifier: a reading of the current sentence under which §10 and the preamble have the same membership either way.

finding: §2.1 excludes table rows from prose, so no table cell can ever be a floor unit, and §8 settles that a reader-added row "never enter[s] the denominator". Composed, a claim living in a table is structurally outside the coverage obligation: it can be dispositioned only as a reader-added row, which moves neither numerator nor denominator, and §11 row 15's mutant forbids the alternative ("count reader-added rows in the numerator"). On this spec that removes 56 table rows from the obligation, including every figure §1.1's pilot argument rests on (17/10/17 claims, 3/1/3 refuted), the seven kind-to-minimum-tier bindings of §4.1, and all 17 test rows. The pilot's own headline defect was a table cell — "a spec asserted *most `PASS` rows carry an empty note* where the corpus says 97% carry one" (§1.1) — so the release's motivating example is in the class its floor cannot reach. The spec never says what a unit owes for a table cell, which leaves the implementer deciding whether tables are out of scope by design or a known gap to report.
suggestion: Say which it is in §2.1. If tables are deliberately out of scope, say so beside the exclusion and note it in Non-Goal 5 so a reader is not left inferring it. If they are not, the cheap fix is a fourth arm over table CELLS (not rows) restricted to cells carrying a digit, which keeps the emitted anchor shape unchanged — and then the pilot's own defect is inside the floor rather than outside it.

finding: §2.2 rests the anchors decision on a premise about tp's shipped behaviour: 'a `ground` command that inlined most of the document would be the one tp command contradicting' the sentence `tp review` emits at `internal/cli/review.go:1778`. Measured by running `tp review spec/1.0.0.md --role ax-economist` on the current tree: the emitted role prompt is 14,197 bytes, of which the 'Changed sections since round 1' block is **8,089 bytes** — a list of changed headings followed by their new content, inlined, capped at 40 lines per section and 6,000 characters total (`diffBlockTotalCharCap`, `internal/cli/review_autodiff.go:15`). So `tp review` already inlines up to 6 KB of the spec into every one of five role prompts per round while emitting the sentence that says it does not, and `tp ground` would not be the one command contradicting it — it would be the second. This is §3's `PARTIAL` / `reason-not-conclusion` exactly: the conclusion holds (anchors are right, and the 2.89× saving is measured) while the stated reason does not. Falsifier: a `tp review` invocation whose prompt carries no inlined section content — the block is emitted whenever a prior snapshot exists and any section changed, so only round 1 qualifies.
suggestion: Replace the premise with the measurement that survives: emitting the floor inline would cost 16,358 B against 5,669 B as anchors on this file (2.89×), recurring every round, while the unit reads the spec file anyway — that argument needs no claim about which other command does what. If the precedent is kept, state it accurately: `tp review` inlines a capped diff block and a section outline, and `tp ground` declines to inline the whole floor for the same reason the cap exists. What the row cannot carry: the wrong reason here is load-bearing beyond this section, because a release that later 'fixes the inconsistency' by making `tp ground` match `tp review` would be inlining, which is the decision this section exists to prevent.

finding: Round 1 falsified "fires **zero times across all sixteen pending specs**" because this file is one of the sixteen and fires once. The repair subtracted one from sixteen rather than recounting, and landed on a second wrong number: "fires **zero times across the fifteen pending specs other than this one**". There are **sixteen** other pending specs, not fifteen. Measured with `/tmp/tp-dev/tp lint --json`, counting `vague-language` findings: 0 on each of 1.38.0, 1.39.0, 1.40.0, 1.41.0, 1.43.0, 1.44.0, 1.45.0, 1.46.0, 1.47.0, 1.48.0, 1.49.0, 1.50.0, 1.51.0, 1.52.0, 1.53.0 and **0.37.1** — sixteen files — and 1 on `spec/1.0.0.md`. The sixteen the repair reasoned from is §1.2's RENAME count (`git show --name-status e73788ab -- 'spec/*.md'` → 16 renames, confirmed), and 0.37.1 is a pending spec that was never renamed, so the two sets differ by exactly the one file the arithmetic lost. This is the repository's own recorded failure shape: a quantifier over a set the author did not enumerate, in the paragraph that argues the cheap ambiguity tier finds nothing.
suggestion: Write "zero times across the sixteen pending specs other than this one, and once on this file", or drop the cardinality and say "zero times on every pending spec but this one" — the claim needs no count, and §2.1's own rule against self-referential figures argues for the countless form.

finding: §2.3 says `vague-language` "fires **zero times across the fifteen pending specs other than this one**". Measured with the dev binary — `tp lint <spec> --json`, counting findings with `rule == vague-language` — over every pending spec: 0 on `0.37.1`, `1.38.0`, `1.39.0`, `1.40.0`, `1.41.0`, `1.43.0`, `1.44.0`, `1.45.0`, `1.46.0`, `1.47.0`, `1.48.0`, `1.49.0`, `1.50.0`, `1.51.0`, `1.52.0`, `1.53.0` — that is **sixteen** files, not fifteen — and 1 on `spec/1.0.0.md`. Fifteen is §1.2's *minor-preserving rename* count ("The move renamed sixteen specs, fifteen of them minor-preserving"), reused as a pending count; `0.37.1` is pending and was not renamed, so the two sets differ by exactly one. The conclusion holds — zero everywhere but this file — and only the quantifier is wrong, which is this repository's most-repeated defect shape and the one CLAUDE.md forbids by name. I am the source of the error: my round-1 suggestion proposed the wording "fifteen other pending specs" and the repair adopted it verbatim, so this is a partial withdrawal of my own round-1 remedy rather than a fresh discovery.
suggestion: Falsifier: a definition of "pending" that excludes `0.37.1` — the roadmap lists it as pending and §1.1 grounds it as a pilot spec, so there is none. Do not replace the number with another number. Bind the claim to its derivation, as this repository's rule requires: state the command (`for f in spec/0.37.1.md spec/1.*.md; do tp lint "$f" --json | jq '[.findings[]|select(.rule=="vague-language")]|length'; done`) and the result shape ("zero on every pending spec but this one, where it fires once on quoted material"), so the sentence cannot rot when the pending set next changes size — which §1.2 says it already did once.

finding: §3 justifies `NOT-A-CLAIM` on an uncounted quantifier — 'it is the majority disposition' and 'most floor units are not claims' — and §2.2 uses the same shape ('the three arms catch most of a document'). Nothing derives either, and the two are different measurements: recall over the document's sentences versus precision over its claims. Measured what can be: applying §2.1's arms to the two pilot specs that have never been edited since creation (`spec/1.52.0.md` and `spec/1.53.0.md`, one commit each) emits **42 floor units**, against the **27 claims** §1.1 says the pilot enumerated by hand on those two files — 1.56 floor units per hand-enumerated claim. That is consistent with non-claims being a minority, not a majority. The bound is not tight, and I say so: it holds only if every hand-enumerated claim is also a floor unit, and §2.2 states the floor misses claims. So the honest reading is that the nearest available evidence does not support the quantifier and nobody has counted. Falsifier: dispositioning one pilot spec's floor and reporting the split — e.g. 'on spec/1.53.0.md the floor emits 18 units of which 8 are not claims' — which is one pass and settles it in either direction. §2.1 already refused to quote a self-referential figure for exactly this reason.
suggestion: Drop 'the majority disposition' and 'most floor units are not claims' and keep the argument that does not need a count: without a recordable value for a non-claim, a conforming run leaves those units blank and coverage is never reachable, whatever their share. That argument is already in §3's next sentence and it is complete on its own. If the share matters — and it does for §9, which says 'the false-positive rate of ungrounded is unknown' — derive it on one pilot spec and state the derivation rather than the adjective; the AX consequence is the per-round obligation, which is 84 dispositions on this file whether the ceremony share is 36% or 60%.

finding: The repair replaced the only §11 row that pointed at isolation (baseline row 10, "the working tree is byte-identical after a ground round that built and ran a probe") and, in the same repair, introduced a new emitted constant — a `tp ground` isolation clause, "a third constant beside the two v0.36.0 §2.2 defines, appended together with `incrementalClause` unchanged" — with no §11 row over it at all. §4.2 makes three assertions a test could read back: that the ground suffix exists and differs from `clauseSuffix()`; that it permits writing inside a copy outside the repository; and that it forbids every write inside the repository except the round's output file. None is asserted. This is the release's only change to a byte-pinned emitted artifact, and v0.36.0 spent four failed drafts establishing that such a suffix needs a positional assertion rather than a containment one (§6.2.1 property 3). Replacing an unfailable row is right; replacing it with nothing over the artifact the repair invented leaves the isolation decision entirely unpinned.
suggestion: Add a row over the ground suffix in property 3's positional form: an emitted ground prompt with a non-empty `output_path` ends with the ground construction exactly, and the same body with those bytes removed does not; mutant — reuse `clauseSuffix()`, which re-emits "report it with its evidence instead of making the edit" and forbids the probe §4.1's tier table requires.

finding: §4.2 makes two claims about v0.36.0 and neither survives reading it — the same class the grounding pass refuted on this file's previous isolation-clause paragraph (`spec/working-map.md`: "A precedent citation is a claim, and this one was inverted... Grounding a citation means reading what it cites"). (a) "a third constant beside the two v0.36.0 §2.2 defines": §2.2 defines ONE clause. `internal/cli/clauses.go:5` says "The two clauses v0.36.0 §2 **and §3** append", and v0.36.0 §6.2.1 property 1 spells the construction as "§2.2's clause, `LF LF`, §3.2's clause" — `isolationClause` is §2.2 (clauses.go:19), `incrementalClause` is §3.2 (clauses.go:23). (b) "v0.36.0 §6.2's byte-for-byte suffix assertion is over the review and audit suffix and is untouched": property 1's text quantifies over emitted prompts, not over commands — "**Every emitted prompt whose `output_path` is non-empty** ends with §2.3's construction exactly ... Holds for `tp review` and `tp audit`" — and property 3 repeats that subject. A `tp ground` prompt names an output file (§7.2), so on property 1's own wording the new suffix falsifies it. What is genuinely untouched is the shipped TEST, which is narrower than the property: `clause_once_test.go` runs over a relocated `spec/0.36.0.md` and the review/audit emissions only. Asserting the property is untouched, when only its test is, is the inverted-precedent shape again.
suggestion: Fix the citation to "a third constant beside §2.2's and §3.2's". Then say what is actually true of §6.2: property 1 as worded covers every prompt with a non-empty `output_path`, so this release either restricts it to `tp review`/`tp audit` (a stated amendment to a shipped property) or gives ground its own positional property. Do not rest the claim on the current test's narrower scope without saying that is what it rests on.

finding: §6's three-to-five ranked causes are now scoped to `QUESTION` (a round-1 repair), but §3 gives `QUESTION` two shapes and the rule fires on both: (a) 'the attempt failed ambiguously' and (b) 'it succeeded below the claim's minimum tier'. Shape (b)'s cause is not unknown — it is recorded on the same row, in `kind` and `tier`, and §4.1 says so: '`QUESTION` is precisely how a unit records that it could not reach the tier'. Ranking three to five falsifiable hypotheses about why a claim is unsettled, when the row already states that it is unsettled because the run was not done, produces exactly what §6 calls a vibe: causes invented to fill a required array. Priced: a QUESTION row with 5 `{cause, prediction}` pairs at 60/80 characters is 987 B against a NOT-A-CLAIM row's 92 B and a PASS row's 159 B, and against a 67 B anchor — a 14.6× divergence between what the emit costs and what the record costs, on the row class this release exists for (§3: 'The second shape is the one this release exists for'). Eight shape-(b) rows on an 84-unit floor is ~7.9 KB of causes, more than the entire anchor payload. Falsifier: a decision the reader of a shape-(b) row makes that ranked causes feed. The decision it feeds is 'go run it at the required tier', which `kind` and `tier` already determine.
suggestion: Scope `causes` in §7.2 to shape (a): required iff the verdict is QUESTION and the attempt was made and was ambiguous; for shape (b), `kind` + `tier` + `evidence` is the cause and `causes` is absent. That needs a discriminator on the row — the same one-enum move §3 already makes for `partial_kind`, e.g. `question_kind: ambiguous | below-tier` — and §11 row 8's 2/3/5/6 boundary test then asserts against shape (a) only. This costs one enum and removes three to five invented hypotheses from every wrong-tier row, which is the row the release is built to produce.

finding: A `--record` file that is present and readable but holds a line that is not JSON has no exit code. §7.1 assigns: 1 to "an unknown enum value, a missing required field, or a tier below its kind's minimum" — all field-level, all presupposing a parsed object; 2 to usage; 3 to "the spec file or the `--record` file is missing or unreadable" — the file is neither; 4 to "the state directory is unreadable or holds a malformed ground round" — the malformed artifact is the input file, not the state directory. This is the same case I named by name in round 1 (`exit-codes-undefined` listed "a `--record` file holding an unparseable line"); the repair enumerated four other paths and left this one out, and it is the likeliest failure in practice because the producer is an agent writing NDJSON incrementally into a file that may be truncated mid-line by a killed run — the incremental-write clause makes a partially written file the expected shape, not the exceptional one.
suggestion: Extend code 1 to cover it: "1 — a row fails validation: a line that is not JSON, an unknown enum value, a missing required field, or a tier below its kind's minimum". Say what happens to a trailing partial line specifically, since §7.2's atomicity rule means one bad line discards the whole round and a truncated final line would throw away a complete run's work.

finding: Exit code 2's rule cannot be coded from its text: "**2** usage, including `--record` without `--status`'s companion flags". `--record` is not a `--status` mode — §7.1's table lists them as separate invocations — and `--status`'s only companion in that table is `--check`, which `--record` has no reason to carry. Read literally the sentence says a bare `tp ground <spec> --record <file>` is a usage error, which contradicts the table row directly above it. §11 row 14 requires "each of 0/1/2/3/4 is produced by a named input, one test per code", so the test for code 2 has to name an input this sentence does not supply.
suggestion: Replace it with the flag combinations that are actually illegal, one per clause — most likely `--check` without `--status`, `--record` together with `--status`, and `--record` with no file argument. Whatever the set, it must be a list a test can enumerate, since row 14 asserts one input per code.

finding: The emitted prompt must name an output file and the spec never names it. §4.2's ground isolation clause "forbids every write inside it except the round's own output file", §11 row 4 asserts what the prompt carries without mentioning it, and the shipped machinery keys on it: `appendClausesReview`/`appendClausesAudit` (`internal/cli/clauses.go:48,61`) append the suffix only to prompts whose `OutputPath` is non-empty, and the comment says the predicate is the output path rather than the role deliberately. So a ground prompt with no output path would silently receive no clause at all — including the ground clause §4.2 requires. Review derives the name from the role (`review-r2-implementer.ndjson`); ground has one prompt and no role (§7.1, Non-Goal 4), so no existing convention supplies it. The payload shape of the emit invocation is likewise unstated: §11 row 4 asserts the prompt carries the anchors and the spec path, and nothing says what JSON envelope carries the prompt or whether it mirrors `tp review`'s `prompts[]` array.
suggestion: Name the output file in §7.1 (`ground-rN.ndjson` is the shape consistent with review's `review-rN-<role>.ndjson` minus the role) and say the ground prompt carries it in the same `output_path` field, so the clause-append predicate keeps working unchanged.

finding: §7.1's exit-code paragraph says "**2** usage, including `--record` without `--status`'s companion flags". Read literally against the table three lines above it, that makes row 2 — `tp ground <spec> --record <file>`, "validates and records the round" — a usage error, because that invocation carries none of `--status`'s companion flags. `--record` and `--status` are alternative rows of the same table, not composable, so no reading makes both sentences true. The intended rule is almost certainly "`--check` without `--status`", which is the shipped pattern elsewhere and matches row 4. This is not a nit in context: §1.2 makes 1.0.0 the release that promises for all of `1.x` that "an exit code already assigned to an outcome keeps that outcome", and §7.1's table is the artifact that assignment is read from. Row 14 pins "each of 0/1/2/3/4 is produced by a named input" — an implementer building row 14's exit-2 input from this sentence writes the test that certifies the contradiction.
suggestion: Falsifier: an invocation that is simultaneously legal in the table and a usage error under the prose — none exists. Rewrite as "**2** usage: an unknown flag, `--check` without `--status`, `--record` without a file argument, or `--record` and `--status` together", and name in row 14 which of those the exit-2 input is, so the row cannot be satisfied by whichever one the implementer happens to pick.

finding: An `UNVERIFIABLE` row is buildable but carries nothing that can be checked. Under §7.2's matrix it requires `kind`, forbids `tier` (iff PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL) and therefore forbids `evidence` (iff `tier` present), leaving `note` — optional free text — as the only place a unit can say what it tried. §3 says UNVERIFIABLE "never gates and never blocks coverage" and §8 says it "counts as dispositioned". Composed: UNVERIFIABLE is a zero-cost, zero-evidence verdict that increments coverage, and a run that answers every floor unit with it reaches 100% having established nothing. §3 anticipates exactly this shape in the other direction — "a verdict absent from the vocabulary is a verdict a unit will fake as `PASS`" — and the repair created the verdict a unit will fake instead. §3 also records that it has zero pilot instances, so nothing calibrates its rate. I file this as medium rather than high because it does not block a task: the validator is codeable as stated. What it costs is the gate.
suggestion: Require `evidence` on UNVERIFIABLE, defined as the attempt that failed and why no higher tier is obtainable (§4.2's worked case — "a claim whose probe would need a package-internal symbol" — is exactly what that field would hold). Optionally add `attempted_tier`. And report UNVERIFIABLE as its own count in `--status` beside the reader-added count, so a run leaning on it is visible without being refused (Non-Goal 3 is untouched by a count).

finding: `anchor` is required on every row and typed as "the `§n(.n)*` section the unit sits in", and this file's own floor contains units for which no such value exists. §2.1 defines prose as "every line of the file except fenced blocks, headings, table rows and list markers" — blockquotes are not excluded. Lines 3-7 of this spec are a blockquote sitting BEFORE `## 1. Overview`: "It was written from **three pilot runs over 44 claims**" (digit arm), "`UNVERIFIABLE` has zero pilot instances (§3)" (backtick arm and digit arm), "§7's storage decision rests on a probe rather than on a pilot run" (backtick arm). Those are floor units under all three arms, they sit in no numbered section, and §7.2 gives `anchor` no legal value for them — so a conforming run cannot record a disposition for them, and §8 then counts them in the denominator forever and `--check` can never exit 0 on this document. The same subsection is where the run must also disposition line 28, which is a VERBATIM QUOTE of another artifact's text (`tp review`'s own framing sentence) emitted as a claim of this spec — a second shape §2.1's prose rule does not distinguish, and the twin of the self-reference §2.3 already records for `vague-language`.
suggestion: Falsifier: a spec in the pending set whose every prose line sits under a numbered heading — this file is not one, and its own title block is the counterexample. Two things are needed and neither is a new mechanism: give §2.1 an explicit rule for blockquote lines (in the floor, or excluded like fenced blocks — the quoted-artifact case argues for excluding them, and it would also close §2.3's self-reference), and give §7.2's `anchor` a defined value for prose above the first heading (a `§0` sentinel or `null`, typed like `unit_id` already is). Add a row: a spec whose first prose line precedes any heading emits a floor whose every unit has a recordable `anchor`.

finding: `anchor` — 'the §n(.n)* section the unit sits in' — is required on every row, but tp can derive it from `line`, which it emits, against the snapshot it writes. tp already does exactly this mapping: the `structured_elements` payload attributes every table and list to its heading ('Table \'1.1 The pilot\' (line 37, 3 rows)'), and `engine.DiffSections` computes section membership for `--diff-from`. Requiring it on the row spends a per-unit lookup ×84 (scan upward for the nearest heading, then translate `### 2.1 The floor` into `§2.1`) plus ~7 B/row, and buys one thing tp does not want: a channel for the row's section to disagree with tp's own parse. A unit that writes `§2` where tp would say `§2.1` produces a row that reports and clusters under a different section, and nothing detects it. Falsifier: a case where tp cannot map an emitted `line` to a section — a unit inside no heading, or a line whose section is ambiguous. §2.1 excludes headings from prose, so every prose unit sits under exactly one; I found no such case.
suggestion: Derive `anchor` at record from `line` + the snapshot, and keep it required only for reader-added rows where `unit_id` is null and tp has no line to derive from. If it is kept on the row for floor units, emit it in the anchor tuple as well so the unit copies rather than derives — the same shape as the `text_sha` fix, and the two together cost 1,596 B (+28%) on this spec's 5,669 B payload while removing 168 per-unit derivations and two silent-disagreement channels per round.

finding: §7.3 says "`roundNumberRe` (`internal/engine/bookkeeping.go:24`) is likewise left alone; ground round numbers are parsed by ground's own list." That is true of ground's NUMBERING and false of the other consumer, which §7.3's prefix analysis does not reach. `roundNumberRe` feeds `roundRefFromName` (`bookkeeping.go:100`), called from `DeriveBookkeeping` (`:57`) for EVERY dirty path under `.tp-review/` — the classifier `tp commit`/`tp done` use to report tp-owned bookkeeping to the operator. Ran the regex `(?:review|audit|snapshot)-round-(\d+)` against the names §7.3 introduces: `review-round-1.ndjson` -> ref `1`, `audit-round-12.ndjson` -> ref `12`, `snapshot-round-3.md` -> ref `3`, but `ground-round-1.ndjson` -> ref `ground-round-1.ndjson` and `snapshot-ground-round-1.md` -> ref `snapshot-ground-round-1.md`, because `roundRefFromName` falls through to the base name on no match. Non-Goal 7 states the round file and its snapshot are written by design, so they are dirty at precisely the moment bookkeeping is derived, and the operator sees a ref of a different shape from every other round artifact. §7.3 enumerated `roundFilePrefixes`, `snapshotPrefixes`, `hasRecordedRoundFiles`, `hasStateArtifacts` and `roundNumberRe`'s numbering use; the bookkeeping use is the one member of that set nobody listed, and §11 has no row on either side of it.
suggestion: Falsifier: `DeriveBookkeeping` not reaching ground artifacts — refuted, it classifies on the `.tp-review/` path prefix (`bookkeeping.go:53`) and takes everything under it. Take the decision explicitly in §7.3: either widen the alternation to `(?:review|audit|snapshot|ground)-round-` and say the ref is the round number like every sibling, or state that the basename ref is deliberate and why. Then add a row asserting the ref a dirty `ground-round-1.ndjson` produces, because whichever is chosen is currently unpinned and an implementer will decide it silently.

finding: §7.3's reason for keeping ground out of both prefix lists is stated as: "`hasRecordedRoundFiles` and `hasStateArtifacts` must be **unchanged** by a ground round, or a spec that has been ground but never reviewed would read as having review state — **which changes the phase the oracle reports** and breaks Non-Goal 1."
